title: Hybrid priority queue with kernel-adaptive admission scheduler for prefill/decode tail isolation
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: Implement a hybrid priority queue plus kernel-adaptive admission scheduler that reduces decode tail latency and improves overall token throughput by aligning admission decisions with kernel suitability and attention-window characteristics. The feature targets workloads with mixed short-chat and long-prefill patterns where naive batching causes p99 spikes and unfair tenant interference.

Context and motivation: Continuous batching in the serving runtime currently uses conservative admission and shape heuristics that do not account for model kernel performance profiles (e.g., attention kernel variants, kv-cache layout) or mixed prefill/decode transitions. This leads to pathological cases where a single large prefill blocks a hardware-optimized small-kernel decode batch causing tail latency regressions and higher unit cost. Our goal is to make admission decisions aware of both request shape and likely kernel choice, and introduce a hybrid queue that separates and then opportunistically merges batches to preserve throughput while bounding p95/p99 latency for latency-sensitive tenants.

Goals:
- Reduce p99 decode latency by >=20% for mixed prefill/decode workloads in hosted clusters.
- Keep aggregate token throughput within 5% of baseline (no regressions >5%).
- Provide per-tenant tail isolation knobs (soft budget + priority buckets).
- Allow kernel affinity hints from model catalog to influence admission and merge policies.

Non-goals:
- Replacing global scheduler; this is an admission layer intended to sit in front of the existing batcher/runtime.
- Solving scheduling for heterogeneous GPUs in a single instance (future work).

Design overview:
1) Hybrid queue: incoming requests are classified into 3 runtime buckets: latency-critical (interactive decode), throughput-prefill (long prefill), and neutral. Each bucket has independent sub-queues and a small admission token bucket (soft budget) to limit inflow.
2) Kernel-adaptive admission: model metadata exposes a small set of kernel affinity tags (e.g., ATTN_FUSED_SMALL, ATTEN_SPLIT_CHUNK, KV_LAYOUT_CONTIG). The admission controller consults a lightweight cost model (latency estimate + token cost) to decide whether to accept into immediate decode batch, delay to form a more efficient batch, or route to background pooling.
3) Opportunistic merge: when hardware is idle and latency budgets allow, the system can merge compatible small-latency and neutral requests if kernel affinity and sequence-length distributions match. Merging uses conservative fallback checks to avoid p99 regressions.
4) Prefill-aware decode isolation: prefill requests are tagged and their KV cache placement is noted; admission avoids mixing conflicting KV-placement types in the same batch where it costs extra memcpy/format conversions.
5) Telemetry + dynamic thresholds: dashboards will surface admission rejects, queue depth per bucket, kernel mismatch events, and per-tenant tail metrics. Thresholds are tuned via automated feedback loop (simple PID controller) to hit p95/p99 targets.

Metrics and acceptance criteria:
- p95 and p99 latency for decode-only flows: target p99 improvement >=20% on mixed workloads.
- Throughput (tokens/sec) within -5% of baseline for 95% of traffic mixes.
- Admission reject rate < 0.5% for standard SLAs; higher for low-priority tenants as configured.
- Per-tenant fairness: no tenant should see >2x relative degradation compared to baseline in canary traffic.

Implementation plan:
- Spike (done): microbenchmarks to measure kernel switching cost across representative models (Llama variants, mix of fused and split-attention kernels). Documented in design doc.
- Prototype admission service (week 1-2): implement hybrid queue + cost model stub; run in local runtime harness.
- Canary rollout (week 3): A/B traffic on a subset of dedicated clusters with synthetic mixed workloads and a few opt-in customers.
- Observability + tuning (week 4): add dashboards, automated threshold tuning, and run for 1 week of production-like traffic before broad rollout.

Rollout plan and safety:
- Feature gated by runtime-config flag and per-cluster opt-in.
- Start with non-critical clusters and internal tenants only.
- Gradual increase with SLO gates: abort rollout if p99 decode latency regresses >5% vs control or if token throughput drops >10% for 10m window.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for admission decisions and cost model logic.
- Integration tests with runtime harness that simulates differing kernel costs and KV layouts.
- Chaos test: inject delayed kernel path and observe failover to fallback merging pathway.
- Perf test: run a 24-hour mixed workload replay against baseline and prototype to measure p95/p99 and throughput.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Complexity: adding kernel affinity and multiple queues increases scheduling complexity and maintenance burden. Mitigation: keep the cost model small and well-documented, and start with conservative defaults.
- Overhead: additional queuing layers may add small queuing latency for throughput-focused workloads; mitigate with opportunistic merging and dynamic thresholds.
- Model metadata freshness: kernel affinity hints must be kept up-to-date by model onboarding. We'll add validation checks to the model catalog pipeline.

Next steps:
- Finalize cost model parameters (latency vs token cost weights).
- Land prototype PR and run internal perf replay.
- Schedule canary with runtime ops and select customers.

comments: Marco Chen: Spiked different kernel-affinity heuristics; we should expose a model metadata flag rather than hardcoding rules.
Sofia Martinez (PM): Need UX for per-tenant priority configuration in Console; added as follow-up.
Design feedback: prefer conservative merging policy for first rollout; avoid merging when KV_LAYOUT differs.
Infra review: add circuit-breaker to disable opportunistic merges when GPU util > 85% to prevent overload.
notes: We intentionally decoupled admission from the runtime kernel selection path to keep runtime hot code minimal.
If successful, next phase will explore co-scheduling hints for multi-GPU shards and automatic kernel selection at the runtime layer.
